subject: Science

unit.unitOverview: Look around your home for a moment. When your mother pours milk into a warm pot and it slowly turns into thick, creamy yoghurt, something has changed. When your father lights the charcoal in the stove and the black lumps glow red and turn to grey ash, something has changed. When you drop a spoon of sugar into your hot shaah (tea) and stir until it disappears, something has changed. Every single day, all around you, materials are changing. Some of these changes can be undone, and some can never be undone again. This unit is all about understanding why materials change, how we can tell a change has happened, and whether we can get the original material back.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, experiments and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

objectives.text: Distinguish between reversible and irreversible changes
Explore how solids can be mixed and how it is often possible to separate them again
Observe, describe, record and begin to explain changes that occur when some solids are added to water
Explore how, when solids do not dissolve or react with water, they can be separated by filtering, which is similar to sieving
Explore how some solids dissolve in water to form solutions and, although the solid cannot be seen, the substance is still present

objectives.subStrand: Ideas and evidence; Plan investigative work
objectives.text: Identify factors that are relevant to a particular situation

outcomes: By the end of this unit, you will be able to:
Tell the difference between a reversible change and an irreversible change, and give clear examples of each from your own life.
Explain the difference between a physical change and a chemical change, and describe the evidence that a new material has been made.
Describe what mixtures and solutions are, and how they are different from pure substances.
Investigate and choose the right method to separate a mixture, such as filtering, evaporating, sieving, or using a magnet.
Use particle theory — the idea that everything is made of tiny particles — to explain melting, dissolving, and other changes.
Identify the factors that make a solid dissolve faster, such as heat, stirring, and grinding into smaller pieces.
Connect what you learn to real life in your community, from rusting roofs to making yoghurt and collecting salt.

Before we begin, here are the important words for this unit. Do not try to memorise them all at once. You will meet each one many times, and they will start to feel familiar. Keep coming back to this table whenever you forget a word.
A change that can be undone, so you can get the original material back.

concepts.title: Two Big Families of Change
concepts.explanation:
Every change you can think of belongs to one of two big families. The first family is reversible changes. These are changes you can undo, so the material goes back to how it started. The second family is irreversible changes. These are changes you cannot undo — once they happen, the material is different forever, and often a completely new material has been made.

Let us think about water. When Amina puts water in the freezer, it turns into hard ice. This is a change — the water went from liquid to solid. But is it reversible? Yes! If she takes the ice out and leaves it in the warm Mogadishu air, it melts straight back into water. Nothing was lost, and nothing new was made. Melting and freezing are reversible changes.

Now think about canjeero. When Khadija pours the runny, sour batter onto the hot pan, it bubbles, sets, and becomes soft, spongy bread. Can she ever turn that cooked canjeero back into runny batter? No, never. Cooking has made a new material with new properties — it looks different, feels different, and tastes different. Cooking is an irreversible change.

The easiest test to remember is this: ask yourself, "Can I get the exact original material back?" If the answer is yes, the change is reversible. If the answer is no, and especially if a new material seems to have appeared, the change is irreversible.

It also helps to know that reversible changes are usually about energy going in and out. When you add heat, ice melts; when you take heat away, water freezes again. The change follows the energy back and forth. Irreversible changes are different: once the new material is made, taking the energy away does not bring the old material back. A burnt log stays as ash no matter how much it cools. Holding on to this idea — reversible changes can go both ways, irreversible changes only go one way — will help you sort almost any change you meet.

Did You Know? A fried egg cannot be turned back into a raw egg no matter how much you cool it down. But melted candle wax or melted ghee will happily turn solid again when it cools. The difference is that cooking the egg made a brand new material, while melting the wax only changed its state.

Here are some reversible changes you already know: melting ghee in a hot pan, freezing water into ice, dissolving sugar or salt in water, boiling water into steam and letting the steam cool back into water, and squashing soft dough into a new shape. In every one of these, you could get the starting material back if you tried.
concepts.example: And here are some irreversible changes you already know: baking bread and canjeero, burning charcoal or firewood, frying meat and eggs, milk turning sour or becoming yoghurt, and iron tools going rusty. In every one of these, a new material has been made and there is no way back.

concepts.title: Physical Changes and Chemical Changes
concepts.explanation:
Scientists have a more exact way of talking about the two families of change. They use the words physical change and chemical change. These are closely linked to reversible and irreversible, so once you understand one, the other becomes easy.

A physical change only changes how a material looks or what state it is in — solid, liquid, or gas. No new material is made. If you crush a lump of rock salt into powder, it is still salt. If you melt a block of ghee, it is still ghee, just in liquid form. If you tear a sheet of paper into small pieces, every piece is still paper. Physical changes are usually reversible, because the material itself has not truly changed — only its shape or state.

A chemical change is deeper. During a chemical change, the tiny particles rearrange themselves and join up in new ways, making one or more new materials with different properties. When Yusuf lights the charcoal, the black carbon joins with invisible oxygen from the air and turns into new gases and grey ash. The ash is nothing like the charcoal we started with. That is a chemical change, and it cannot be undone.

Because you cannot see the tiny particles moving, scientists look for clues or evidence that a chemical change has happened. Watch out for these signs:

A colour change — shiny grey iron slowly turns orange-brown when it rusts.

A gas is made — bubbles fizz up when vinegar meets baking soda, even though you added no air.

Heat or light is given out — burning charcoal glows and feels hot; this heat cooks your food.

A new smell — the smell of frying meat or baking bread comes from brand new materials.

A change that will not reverse — once the new material is made, you cannot get the old one back.

If you see one or more of these clues, you are almost certainly watching a chemical change. If you see none of them and the material only changed shape or state, it is probably a physical change.
concepts.example: Did You Know? When milk becomes yoghurt, tiny helpful living things called bacteria change the milk sugar into acid. That acid makes the milk thick and gives yoghurt its sour taste — a real chemical change happening in your kitchen. This is why yoghurt (caano fadhi) can never be turned back into fresh milk.

concepts.title: Rusting, Burning, and Cooking
concepts.explanation:
Three of the most important irreversible changes in your life are rusting, burning, and cooking. Let us look at each one closely, because they show up everywhere in your community.

Along the humid coast near Mombasa, Berbera, and Lamu, you will see metal roofs, nails, gates, and fishing hooks slowly turning orange and crumbly. This is rusting. Rust forms when iron meets both water and oxygen from the air over time. The iron joins with the oxygen to make a new orange material called iron oxide, which is soft and flaky, not strong like iron. This is why old tools break and roofs get holes. Rusting is a chemical change, and it happens faster where the air is damp and salty, which is exactly why coastal metal rusts quicker than metal in dry Garissa.

People slow down rusting by keeping iron dry, by painting it, or by covering it with oil or grease. A painted gate or an oiled knife lasts much longer, because the paint and oil keep the water and oxygen away from the iron.

When Omar burns charcoal or firewood to cook, the fuel joins with oxygen from the air and gives out heat and light. New materials are made — gases that float away and grey ash that is left behind. You can never turn the ash and smoke back into charcoal, so burning is an irreversible chemical change. Burning is very useful, but it must always be done carefully and with an adult, because fire can spread and the smoke can be harmful to breathe in a closed room.

Cooking is a chemical change that we do on purpose because it makes food safe and tasty. When Sahra fries an egg, the runny clear part turns solid and white forever. When Ibrahim bakes bread or canjeero, the soft dough becomes firm bread. When goat meat roasts over the coals, it changes colour, smell, and texture. None of these can be undone. New materials have been made, and that is what makes cooked food different from raw food.

It is worth noticing that heat causes both reversible and irreversible changes, so heat alone is not the difference. When you heat ghee it melts, and that is reversible — the ghee is still ghee. But when you heat an egg it sets solid forever, and that is irreversible — a new material has formed. The real question is always the same: did a new material appear, or did the material only change its state? Melting the ghee only changed its state, but cooking the egg made something new. Keep this in mind, because it is one of the easiest points to get confused about.
concepts.example: [*] Remember! Rusting, burning, and cooking are all irreversible chemical changes. In each one, a brand new material is made, and there is no way to get the original material back. Look for the clues: new colour, new smell, gas, or heat and light.

concepts.title: Mixtures and Pure Substances
concepts.explanation:
Not every change makes a new material. Sometimes we simply mix materials together. A mixture is two or more materials that are stirred or jumbled together but are not joined chemically. The important thing about a mixture is that each material keeps its own properties, and — here is the key idea — you can usually separate them again.

Think of a bag of rice (bariis) that has small stones mixed in. The rice is still rice and the stones are still stones. They are just sitting together. With patience you can pick out every stone, because nothing new was made. That is a mixture. In the same way, sand mixed with iron filings, or beans mixed with lentils, or tea leaves floating in water, are all mixtures.

A pure substance, on the other hand, is made of only one kind of material, like clean water or pure salt. There is nothing else mixed in. Most things around you are actually mixtures, not pure substances — even the air you breathe is a mixture of several gases, and seawater is a mixture of water and many dissolved salts.
concepts.example: Scientists also talk about two kinds of mixtures. In some mixtures you can clearly see the different parts, like rice and stones, or a fresh salad. These are called heterogeneous mixtures. In other mixtures the parts are spread out so evenly that you cannot see them separately, like salt fully dissolved in water. These even mixtures are called homogeneous mixtures, and a solution is a good example.

concepts.title: Solutions and Dissolving
concepts.explanation:
A solution is a very special kind of mixture. It forms when a solid dissolves completely into a liquid, spreading out so evenly that you cannot see it any more. When you stir sugar into hot shaah and it vanishes, you have made a solution. The tea now tastes sweet, so you know the sugar is still there — it has not disappeared, it has just spread out into tiny particles that are too small to see.

Scientists give the parts of a solution special names. The solid that dissolves is called the solute. The liquid that does the dissolving is called the solvent. And the sweet or salty mixture they make together is the solution. So in a cup of sweet shaah, sugar is the solute, tea is the solvent, and sweet tea is the solution. In seawater, salt is the solute, water is the solvent, and salty water is the solution.

It is very important to understand that dissolving is a reversible change and a physical change. The sugar has not turned into a new material — it is still sugar, just hidden. If you gently heat the solution and let all the water evaporate away, the sugar or salt will be left behind, exactly as it was. This is a wonderful proof that the solute never truly disappeared.

You may have noticed that sugar dissolves much faster in hot shaah than in cold water. Scientists have found three main things that make a solid dissolve faster:

Heat — warming the liquid makes its particles move faster, so they bump into the solute and break it apart more quickly. Sugar melts into hot tea almost at once.

Stirring — stirring with a spoon keeps fresh liquid moving past the solute, carrying the dissolved particles away and speeding things up.

Smaller pieces — crushing or grinding the solid into a fine powder gives the liquid more surface to work on, so it dissolves faster than one big lump.

There is also a limit to how much can dissolve. If Maryam keeps adding salt to a cup of water and stirring, at some point no more salt will dissolve, and extra salt just sits at the bottom. We then say the solution is saturated — it is full and cannot hold any more. Warming the water usually lets a little more dissolve.
concepts.example: Did You Know? When a person is very sick with diarrhoea, doctors give a life-saving drink made by dissolving a little salt and sugar in clean, boiled water. This simple solution, called oral rehydration solution, has saved millions of lives across East Africa and the world. It works because the dissolved salt and sugar spread evenly through every sip, exactly matching what the sick body needs.

concepts.title: Separating Mixtures
concepts.explanation:
Because the materials in a mixture are not chemically joined, we can pull them apart again. This is called separation, and choosing the right method depends on the mixture. Here are the main methods you should know.

Picking or sorting by hand — useful when the pieces are big enough to see, like taking stones out of rice.

Sieving — shaking a mixture through a sieve or mesh lets small pieces fall through while large pieces stay on top, like sifting flour to remove lumps.

Using a magnet — a magnet pulls out iron pieces from a mixture, because only iron and a few metals are magnetic. This separates iron filings from sand.

Filtering — pouring a mixture of liquid and an undissolved solid through cloth or a filter catches the solid and lets the clean liquid through, like straining tea leaves or cleaning muddy water through a cloth.

Evaporating — gently heating a solution until the liquid turns to gas and floats away, leaving the dissolved solid behind. This is exactly how people collect salt from seawater.

The clever part is that you often need more than one method for a tricky mixture. Imagine a mixture of iron filings, sand, and salt. First you use a magnet to pull out the iron. Then you add water so the salt dissolves but the sand does not, and you filter to catch the sand and keep the salty water. Finally you evaporate the salty water to leave pure salt behind. Three methods, one clever plan.

Along the East African coast, people have collected salt this way for hundreds of years. They let seawater flow into shallow pans dug into the ground. The strong sun evaporates the water, and gleaming white salt is left behind to be gathered, dried, and sold. It is a beautiful example of separating a solution using nothing but sunshine.
concepts.example: The most important lesson about separating mixtures is that you must match the method to the material. You cannot use a magnet on salt, because salt is not magnetic. You cannot use a filter to catch dissolved sugar, because the sugar particles slip straight through the tiny holes. And you cannot sieve two powders that are the same size. So before you choose a method, always ask what makes each material special: Is it magnetic? Does it dissolve? Is it big enough to see and pick out? Is it a solid mixed in a liquid? Once you know the properties of each part, the right method almost chooses itself, and that is how scientists and factories plan every separation.

visualModels.title: Separating Mixtures
visualModels.purpose: Because the materials in a mixture are not chemically joined, we can pull them apart again. This is called separation, and choosing the right method depends on the mixture. Here are the main methods you should know.

methods.title: The Fizzing Reaction (Vinegar and Baking Soda)
methods.example: To see the evidence of an irreversible chemical change when vinegar meets baking soda.
steps: Put the two spoons of baking soda into the bottom of the tall glass.
Look closely at the baking soda and the vinegar. Note their colour and whether they are solid or liquid.
Slowly pour the vinegar onto the baking soda and step back a little.
Watch carefully. Note what happens straight away and for the next minute.
Once the fizzing stops, look at what is left in the glass.

methods.title: Growing Rust (Iron Nails Investigation)
methods.example: To find out what iron needs in order to rust, just like the metal roofs and tools along the coast.
steps: Label your three cups A, B, and C.
Cup A: leave a nail dry with nothing added, open to the air.
Cup B: put a nail in and cover it completely with water.
Cup C: put a nail in and cover it completely with cooking oil so no air can reach it.
For an extra test, add a pinch of salt to Cup B to copy the salty coastal air.

methods.title: The Dissolving Speed Race
methods.example: To find out whether heat, stirring, and grinding really do make sugar dissolve faster.
steps: Fill one glass with cold water and one with the same amount of warm water.
At the same moment, drop one level spoon of sugar into each glass. Do not stir.
Time how long the sugar takes to fully disappear in each glass and record it.
Now repeat with two fresh glasses of cold water. In one, stir hard; in the other, do not stir. Time both.
For a final test, compare a whole sugar lump against the same amount of ground-up sugar in two glasses of cold water.

methods.title: Getting Salt Back From Salt Water
methods.example: To prove that dissolving is reversible by separating salt back out of salt water, just as coastal people collect sea salt.
steps: Stir the salt into the warm water until it completely dissolves and you cannot see it any more.
Look at the water — it should be clear. The salt is now a solution.
Pour a thin layer of the salt water into the shallow dish.
Place the dish in a sunny, safe spot where it will not be disturbed.
Leave it for one to three days and check it each day as the water slowly evaporates.

methods.title: Cleaning Muddy Water by Filtering
methods.example: To use filtration to separate solid dirt from water and see how communities clean muddy river water.
steps: Place the cloth or filter inside the funnel, and sit the funnel in the empty cup.
For a better filter, add a layer of clean sand and small stones on top of the cloth.
Slowly pour the muddy water into the filter and watch what drips through.
Compare the water that comes out with the muddy water you started with.
Look at what is left behind on the cloth and sand.

workedExamples.title: Planning a Separation
workedExamples.prompt: Let us work through a separation problem together, step by step, the way a scientist would.
workedExamples.solution:
Problem: Zahra has accidentally mixed together a spoon of sand, a spoon of salt, and some small iron filings in one bowl. She wants to separate all three back into clean, separate piles. How can she do it?

Step 1 — Look at the properties. Iron is magnetic; sand and salt are not. Salt dissolves in water; sand and iron do not. These two facts are the keys to the whole plan.

Step 2 — Remove the iron first. Move a magnet over the dry mixture. The iron filings jump to the magnet, and Zahra lifts them clean away. Now only sand and salt are left.

Step 3 — Dissolve the salt. Add water and stir. The salt dissolves and disappears into the water, but the sand sinks and stays solid. Now she has a mixture of salty water and sand.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 2
workedExamples.prompt: Which of these is a reversible change? (a) Burning charcoal (b) Melting ghee (c) Frying an egg (d) Rusting a nail
workedExamples.solution: (b) Melting ghee. Melting only changes the state; the ghee can be cooled back to solid, so it is reversible. The others all make new materials.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 3
workedExamples.prompt: Which is an irreversible change? (a) Freezing water (b) Dissolving sugar (c) Baking canjeero (d) Melting wax
workedExamples.solution: (c) Baking canjeero. Cooking makes a new material that cannot turn back into batter. Freezing, dissolving, and melting can all be reversed.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 4
workedExamples.prompt: When salt dissolves in water, the salt: (a) disappears forever (b) turns into a new material (c) spreads out between the water particles (d) reacts to make a gas
workedExamples.solution: (c) It spreads out between the water particles. The salt is still there, hidden among the water particles, which is why the water tastes salty and the salt returns when the water evaporates.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 5
workedExamples.prompt: In a cup of sweet shaah, the sugar is the: (a) solvent (b) solute (c) solution (d) mixture
workedExamples.solution: (b) Solute. The solute is the solid that dissolves — here, the sugar.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 6
workedExamples.prompt: In salt water, the water is the: (a) solute (b) solvent (c) solid (d) filter
workedExamples.solution: (b) Solvent. The solvent is the liquid that does the dissolving — here, the water.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 7
workedExamples.prompt: Which tool would separate iron filings from sand? (a) A sieve (b) A filter (c) A magnet (d) Evaporation
workedExamples.solution: (c) A magnet. Iron is magnetic, so a magnet pulls the iron filings out while leaving the sand behind.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 8
workedExamples.prompt: Which method separates salt from salt water? (a) Filtering (b) Using a magnet (c) Evaporation (d) Sieving
workedExamples.solution: (c) Evaporation. Heating the salt water lets the water escape as gas and leaves the salt behind. A magnet and sieve would not work, and a filter cannot catch dissolved salt.

activities.title: The Fizzing Reaction (Vinegar and Baking Soda)
activities.materials: Two spoons of baking soda (bicarbonate of soda); Half a cup of vinegar; A tall clear glass or jar; A small spoon
steps: Put the two spoons of baking soda into the bottom of the tall glass.
Look closely at the baking soda and the vinegar. Note their colour and whether they are solid or liquid.
Slowly pour the vinegar onto the baking soda and step back a little.
Watch carefully. Note what happens straight away and for the next minute.
Once the fizzing stops, look at what is left in the glass.
Safety: Only test safe kitchen liquids such as lemon juice and vinegar. Never touch or mix cleaning products like bleach, and never taste anything you are testing.

activities.title: Growing Rust (Iron Nails Investigation)
activities.materials: Three clean iron nails (steel nails work well); Three small jars or cups; Water; Cooking oil (a few spoonfuls); A little salt (optional, to copy sea air)
steps: Label your three cups A, B, and C.
Cup A: leave a nail dry with nothing added, open to the air.
Cup B: put a nail in and cover it completely with water.
Cup C: put a nail in and cover it completely with cooking oil so no air can reach it.
For an extra test, add a pinch of salt to Cup B to copy the salty coastal air.
Safety: Pins and nails have sharp points — ask an adult to help, and store them safely afterwards.

activities.title: The Dissolving Speed Race
activities.materials: Sugar (loose sugar and, if you have them, a couple of sugar lumps); Two clear glasses; Cold water and warm water (ask an adult to warm it); A spoon for stirring; A clock or timer
steps: Fill one glass with cold water and one with the same amount of warm water.
At the same moment, drop one level spoon of sugar into each glass. Do not stir.
Time how long the sugar takes to fully disappear in each glass and record it.
Now repeat with two fresh glasses of cold water. In one, stir hard; in the other, do not stir. Time both.
For a final test, compare a whole sugar lump against the same amount of ground-up sugar in two glasses of cold water.

activities.title: Getting Salt Back From Salt Water
activities.materials: A spoon of salt; Warm water in a cup; A dark-coloured shallow dish or plate; A sunny windowsill or warm, safe spot
steps: Stir the salt into the warm water until it completely dissolves and you cannot see it any more.
Look at the water — it should be clear. The salt is now a solution.
Pour a thin layer of the salt water into the shallow dish.
Place the dish in a sunny, safe spot where it will not be disturbed.
Leave it for one to three days and check it each day as the water slowly evaporates.

activities.title: Cleaning Muddy Water by Filtering
activities.materials: A cup of muddy water (stir a little clean soil or sand into water); A clean cloth or a coffee filter; An empty cup or jar; A funnel or the top half of a cut plastic bottle (ask an adult to cut it); Optional: clean sand and small clean stones
steps: Place the cloth or filter inside the funnel, and sit the funnel in the empty cup.
For a better filter, add a layer of clean sand and small stones on top of the cloth.
Slowly pour the muddy water into the filter and watch what drips through.
Compare the water that comes out with the muddy water you started with.
Look at what is left behind on the cloth and sand.

activities.title: Observe: Separating Mixtures
activities.materials: Two spoons of baking soda (bicarbonate of soda); Half a cup of vinegar; A tall clear glass or jar; A small spoon
steps: Look for an example of separating mixtures around your home or outside.
Watch it closely for a few minutes and note three things you notice.
Write or draw what you observed, using the words Reversible change and Irreversible change.
Explain your finding out loud, as if you were teaching it. Say it to a family member or your teacher if someone is nearby, or explain it to yourself and check it against the concept explanations.

rules.title: Two Big Families of Change
rules.text: Every change you can think of belongs to one of two big families.

rules.title: Physical Changes and Chemical Changes
rules.text: Scientists have a more exact way of talking about the two families of change.

rules.title: Rusting, Burning, and Cooking
rules.text: Three of the most important irreversible changes in your life are rusting, burning, and cooking.

rules.title: Mixtures and Pure Substances
rules.text: Not every change makes a new material.

rules.title: Solutions and Dissolving
rules.text: A solution is a very special kind of mixture.

rules.title: Separating Mixtures
rules.text: Because the materials in a mixture are not chemically joined, we can pull them apart again.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: What is the difference between a reversible and an irreversible change?

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Name three clues that tell you a chemical change has happened.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Any three of: a colour change, a gas being made, heat or light given out, a new smell, or a change that will not reverse.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain why rusting is an irreversible change.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Rusting is irreversible because the iron joins with oxygen and water to make a new material, iron oxide, which has different properties and cannot be turned back into iron.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: What is the difference between a mixture and a solution?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A mixture is any two or more materials jumbled together; a solution is a special mixture where a solid has dissolved evenly into a liquid so it cannot be seen.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Name the solute, solvent, and solution when you stir salt into water.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The solute is the salt, the solvent is the water, and the solution is the salt water they make together.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: List the three things that make a solid dissolve faster.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Heating the liquid, stirring it, and breaking the solid into smaller pieces.

rounds.explanation: Evaporation. Heating the salt water lets the water escape as gas and leaves the salt behind. A magnet and sieve would not work, and a filter cannot catch dissolved salt.

rounds.prompt: Which is a pure substance?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 3 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Clean water. Pure water is made of only one kind of material. Seawater, air, and rice with stones are all mixtures.

rounds.prompt: Which of these is a reversible change?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 3 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Melting ghee. Melting only changes the state; the ghee can be cooled back to solid, so it is reversible. The others all make new materials.

rounds.prompt: In a cup of sweet shaah, the sugar is the:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 3 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Solute. The solute is the solid that dissolves — here, the sugar.

games.description: Practise solvent through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: Iron needs which two things to rust?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 3 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Water and oxygen. Iron rusts only when both water and oxygen from the air can reach it.

rounds.prompt: Which makes sugar dissolve faster?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 3 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Stirring, heating, and using smaller pieces all speed up dissolving.

rounds.prompt: Which is an irreversible change?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 3 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Baking canjeero. Cooking makes a new material that cannot turn back into batter. Freezing, dissolving, and melting can all be reversed.

rounds.prompt: In salt water, the water is the:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 3 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Solvent. The solvent is the liquid that does the dissolving — here, the water.

games.description: Practise solubility through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: Which of these is a clue that a chemical change has happened?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 3 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: All of these. A new colour, a new gas, and heat or light are all clues that a chemical change has happened.

rounds.prompt: A mixture where you cannot see the separate parts, like salt water, is called:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 3 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Homogeneous. In a homogeneous mixture the parts are spread evenly and cannot be seen separately, like salt water.

rounds.prompt: When salt dissolves in water, the salt:
choices: spreads out between the water particles
rounds.answer: spreads out between the water particles
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 3 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: It spreads out between the water particles. The salt is still there, hidden among the water particles, which is why the water tastes salty and the salt returns when the water evaporates.

rounds.prompt: Which tool would separate iron filings from sand?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 3 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: A magnet. Iron is magnetic, so a magnet pulls the iron filings out while leaving the sand behind.

selfAssessment: I can by the end of this unit, you will be able to:
I can tell the difference between a reversible change and an irreversible change, and give clear examples of each from your own life.
I can explain the difference between a physical change and a chemical change, and describe the evidence that a new material has been made.
I can describe what mixtures and solutions are, and how they are different from pure substances.
I can investigate and choose the right method to separate a mixture, such as filtering, evaporating, sieving, or using a magnet.
I can use particle theory — the idea that everything is made of tiny particles — to explain melting, dissolving, and other changes.
I can identify the factors that make a solid dissolve faster, such as heat, stirring, and grinding into smaller pieces.
I can connect what you learn to real life in your community, from rusting roofs to making yoghurt and collecting salt.
